idiom_name: trait or abstract class with protected provided operations and a protected abstract entry point, overridden with override
implementation_notes: Scala offers the structure directly: a trait or abstract class carries the provided operations as protected defs, the sandbox method is protected abstract, and every concrete behaviour supplies it with override (the Tour of Scala traits page shows exactly this abstract-member/override mechanism, and Scala 3's open modifier documents the intended extension point). Access can be narrowed beyond Kotlin's or Java's vocabulary: protected[this] restricts a primitive to calls on the same instance and protected[package] to a package, so the primitive API can be scoped more tightly than 'class and subclasses' without leaving the language. A trait composes several sandbox fragments into one behaviour, which is the natural Scala alternative when the primitives split across concerns. Use the trait form when behaviours are stateless, an abstract class when they carry constructor parameters or state. What replaces the classic structure when the primitives need no shared state is a parameter object of engine handles passed to a plain function; the trait stays the clearer form when one primitive set is shared by a family that also owns state.
code_sketch:
trait Superpower:                                    // Scala 3 syntax; mark `open` on a class
  protected def activate(): Unit                     // the sandbox method
  protected def playSound(id: SoundId, volume: Double = 1.0): Unit = audio.play(id, volume)
  protected def spawnParticles(kind: ParticleType, count: Int): Unit = fx.spawn(kind, count)

final class SkyLaunch(audio: Audio, fx: Particles) extends Superpower:
  override protected def activate(): Unit =          // composes primitives only
    playSound(SoundId.Sproing)
    spawnParticles(ParticleType.Dust, 10)
pitfalls: Scala lets an override widen visibility, so a subclass can re-publish a protected primitive (or the entry point) as public and hand the vocabulary to its own callers; keep the family under your control or final.

Trait linearisation decides which implementation wins, and a class that mixes in two sandbox traits with a same-named primitive must resolve the clash explicitly (super[A]), which fails confusingly later rather than at the mixin site.
Classes are open by default, so nothing stops an unrelated type from extending the sandbox and bypassing an invariant; seal the family with sealed when the set of behaviours is fixed.

protected[this] and protected[pkg] are easy to over-tighten: a primitive narrowed to the instance cannot be used by a helper the behaviour delegates to, and the error appears as an access error at the call site.
